title: SYSK Selects: How Population Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the November 2009 episode "How Population Works." The hosts introduce it as a pick from the archive. They cover why humans congregate, hunter-gatherer band sizes, natural versus statistical populations, and how demographers study them. Methods discussed include complete enumeration (the census, with its every-ten-years schedule and 72-year secrecy rule) and sampling with margin of error. Other topics are population attributes such as age (the baby boom bulge), socioeconomic data, and race, plus population history: the effect of Columbus and smallpox on the Americas and the Taino decline, growth from about 10,000 BC onward, the Malthusian exponential growth model, replacement rate of 2.3, bottlenecks such as the Plague of Justinian and the Black Death, and founder effect. They also cover population density (Kowloon Walled City), population control (China's one-child policy), and population decline with incentive programs in Russia, Japan, and Australia. The episode closes with listener mail about Toledo and a car with ants.

segments.title: Selects introduction and opening banter
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Selects episode from the 2009 archive as How Population Works. Hosts plug a Road to Punkin Chunkin broadcast on Science Channel and open with jokes about belonging to a population.

segments.title: Why humans congregate and what demographers study
segments.summary: Humans congregate for safety, farming, and cooperation. Hunter-gatherer bands tended to stay around thirty people. Demographers study natural populations by attributes such as party, ethnicity, and poverty, and by segregation patterns.

segments.title: Counting populations: census and sampling
segments.summary: Complete enumeration counts every person, as the census does every ten years, with enumerators going door to door. The census data is kept secret for seventy-two years. Sampling uses a statistical formula and a random sample to estimate the whole population, with a margin of error. Phone-book sampling is criticized as biased.

segments.title: Population attributes: age, socioeconomics, and race
segments.summary: Populations can be grouped by age, location, socioeconomic status, and race. The post-World War Two baby boom is given as an example of an age bulge. Socioeconomic data can reveal health clusters near industrial sites. Race is discussed as a hinky category with limited usefulness, though some medical conditions are race-specific.

segments.title: Columbus, smallpox, and the Americas' population
segments.summary: Charles C. Mann's research suggests the Americas had far more people before European contact than previously thought, about a fifth of the world's population. Smallpox and later violence reduced the population. The hosts discuss Columbus and the Taino on Hispaniola as a case of genocide.

segments.title: Historical population growth, exponential growth, and replacement rate
segments.summary: Estimates show world population rising from about one to ten million around 10,000 BC to fifty million by 1000 BC and two million by 600 CE. It grew to around 500 million by the mid-1400s, and then sharply in the twentieth century. Malthus's exponential growth model is described. The replacement rate, cited as 2.3 children per woman, is explained along with the goal of zero population growth.

segments.title: Bottlenecks, plagues, founder effect, and population density
segments.summary: Bottlenecks such as the Plague of Justinian and the Black Death are discussed, along with genetic bottlenecks and the founder effect. The hosts cover Kowloon Walled City, cited as the highest population density, with about fifty thousand people in one block.

segments.title: Population control, decline, and incentives
segments.summary: The hosts discuss population control through China's one-child policy and the strains of overpopulation on resources. They then turn to population decline in Japan, Russia, and Australia, where governments offer incentives to have babies. Birth control's effect on fertility is also mentioned.

segments.title: Closing and listener mail
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and plug the How Stuff Works article on population. Listener mail covers a Toledo fan's lobbying for a key to the city and a listener whose 1988 Dodge Colt has detached struts and ants.
